title: Prostate, thyroid, contrast and the home page

findings.piece: Page title and reference box (name, version, publisher, application)
findings.says: Title "PI-RADS v2.1 — Prostate MRI Reporting & Data System". Collapsed box: "Full Name: Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System", "Version: 2.1 (2019)", "Publisher: American College of Radiology (ACR) / European Society of Urogenital Radiology (ESUR)", "Application: Multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) of the prostate". The box has no citation; the References list at the foot of the page has three (B2-pi-rads-36).

sources.location: Cover, p. i ("Prostate Imaging – Reporting and Data System", 2019, Version 2.1); Introduction, pp. 1–2 (PDF pp. 8–9): Steering Committee of the ACR, ESUR and the AdMeTech Foundation; p. 3 (PDF p. 10): designed for "patients with suspected cancer in treatment naïve prostate glands"; does not address recurrence after therapy or progression during surveillance
Slide "Major Revisions in PI-RADS v2.1" (DWI scores 2–3, TZ T2W scores 1–2, TZ overall category, DCE negatives, sector map)

findings.fix: The version and full name are right, but the page is not v2.1 throughout: its DWI 2–3 and TZ T2W 1–2 definitions are v2's and its TZ rule matches neither version (B2-pi-rads-04, -11, -15, -17). Fix those, add "treatment-naïve prostate" to Application, name the AdMeTech Foundation beside ACR and ESUR, and use the document's name ("Prostate Imaging – Reporting and Data System") in the title.

findings.piece: Purpose box: definition of clinically significant cancer
findings.says: "PI-RADS v2.1 standardizes mpMRI assessment for clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa), defined as Gleason score ≥ 7 (Grade Group ≥ 2) or tumor volume ≥ 0.5 cc."

sources.location: Section III, p. 10 (PDF p. 17): "Gleason score ≥7 (including 3+4 with prominent but not predominant Gleason 4 component), and/or volume ≥0.5cc, and/or extraprostatic extension (EPE)"
Background and Rationale, p. 2: most widely adopted criterion Gleason ≥3+4, ISUP Grade Group ≥2

findings.fix: Add "and/or extraprostatic extension (EPE)" (p. 10); the Gleason, Grade Group and volume figures are right.

findings.piece: Calculator: peripheral zone path
findings.says: Zone "Peripheral Zone (PZ) — DWI dominant": the result is the DWI score, except DWI 3 with "DCE Positive? Yes" gives 4. Runs (docs/audit/batch-2/cases/pirads.results.md): all 7 PZ cases match v2.1 — DWI 1 with T2W 5 and DCE+ → 1; DWI 2 with DCE+ → 2; DWI 3 DCE− → 3; DWI 3 DCE+ → 4; DWI 4 with T2W 2 → 4; DWI 4 with DCE+ → 4; DWI 5 with T2W 1 → 5.

sources.location: Section III, PI-RADS Assessment, Peripheral Zone table, p. 11 (PDF p. 18); Caveats for Overall Assessment, p. 14 (PDF p. 21) (DWI 4 with T2W 2 is 4); bpMRI commentary, p. 24 (PDF p. 31) (PZ DWI 3 is not upgraded without DCE)

findings.piece: Calculator: transition zone path
findings.says: Zone "Transition Zone (TZ) — T2WI dominant": the result is the T2W score, except T2W 3 with DWI ≥4 gives 4; T2W 2 stays 2 whatever the DWI. Runs (docs/audit/batch-2/cases/pirads.results.md): v21-tz-t2w3-dwi4 → "PI-RADS 4 … Targeted biopsy recommended" (expected 3); v21-tz-t2w2-dwi4 → "PI-RADS 2 … No biopsy recommended" (expected 3); v21-tz-t2w2-dwi5 → 2 (expected 3). v2-tz-t2w3-dwi4 → 4, though v2 also gives 3, so the rule follows neither version. The other 9 TZ cases match (T2W 1 with DWI 5 → 1; T2W 2 with DWI 1 or 3 → 2; T2W 3 with DWI 1, or DWI 3 and DCE+ → 3; T2W 3 with DWI 5 → 4; T2W 4 with DWI 2 → 4; T2W 5 → 5).

sources.location: Section III, PI-RADS Assessment, Transition Zone table, p. 11 (PDF p. 18): T2W 2 with DWI ≤3 → 2, ≥4 → 3; T2W 3 with DWI ≤4 → 3, 5 → 4; Evaluation of the TZ, pp. 13–14 (PDF pp. 20–21) (atypical nodules upgraded to 3 with DWI 4 or more; no upgrade on DWI 3)

Slide "Image Interpretation: Transition Zone" (v2 and v2.1 tables side by side: both give T2W 3 with DWI ≤4 → 3; "The only change in deriving the overall PI-RADS assessment category, compared to PI-RADS v2, concerns TZ lesions with a T2W score of 2")

findings.fix: Apply the v2.1 TZ table: T2W 2 → 3 when DWI is 4 or 5 (otherwise 2); T2W 3 → 4 only when DWI is 5 (otherwise 3).

findings.piece: Calculator: option labels, and no input for an inadequate sequence
findings.says: DWI options "2 — Indistinct hypointensity on ADC", "3 — Focal mild/moderate hypointensity; <1.5 cm"; T2WI options "1 — Normal TZ or round well-defined BPH nodule", "2 — Circumscribed hypointense, well-defined margins"; DCE "Yes — Focal early enhancement" (hint "PZ only: focal early enhancement vs. adjacent tissue"). All four fields are required; none has an option for a sequence that is technically inadequate or not done, and the T2WI hint says it is "not used for PZ scoring".

sources.location: DWI table, p. 20 (PDF p. 27): 2 "Linear/wedge shaped hypointense on ADC and/or linear/wedge shaped hyperintense on high b-value DWI"; 3 "Focal (discrete and different from the background) hypointense on ADC and/or focal hyperintense on high b-value DWI; may be markedly hypointense on ADC or markedly hyperintense on high b-value DWI, but not both" (no size limit); TZ T2W table, p. 18 (PDF p. 25): 1 "round, completely encapsulated nodule", 2 "mostly encapsulated nodule OR a homogeneous circumscribed nodule without encapsulation … OR a homogeneous mildly hypointense area between nodules"; DCE table, p. 22 (PDF p. 29) (positive must correspond to a suspicious T2W and/or DWI finding); category X, p. 15, and the tables for assessment without adequate DWI or DCE, p. 16 (PDF pp. 22–23)
Slides "Image Interpretation: DWI" and "Assessment of T2W" (v2 wording on the left, v2.1 on the right)

findings.fix: Relabel the options with v2.1's wording (DWI 3 has no size limit in either version; a T2W 1 nodule is completely encapsulated, whatever its signal; DCE+ must match a T2W/DWI finding). Add "inadequate / not done" for DWI and DCE that applies the p. 16 tables (without adequate DWI, PZ and TZ are scored on T2W, with DCE+ raising 3 to 4).

findings.piece: Quick Reference: categories and probability
findings.says: "PI-RADS 1 | Very low (essentially no csPCa)", "PI-RADS 2 | Low", "PI-RADS 3 | Intermediate", "PI-RADS 4 | High", "PI-RADS 5 | Very high".

sources.location: Section III, PI-RADS v2.1 Assessment Categories, p. 10 (PDF p. 17); repeated in Appendix I, p. 29 (PDF p. 36)

findings.fix: Optional: for 1, use the document's words ("clinically significant cancer is highly unlikely to be present") rather than "essentially no csPCa".

findings.piece: Quick Reference: action for PI-RADS 1–3 (and the calculator's results for 1–3)
findings.says: "PI-RADS 1 … No biopsy"; "PI-RADS 2 … No biopsy (consider in context)"; "PI-RADS 3 … Biopsy at clinician discretion (consider PSA density, clinical risk)". The calculator's results for 1–3 say the same.

sources.location: Section III, p. 10 (PDF p. 17): biopsy "should be considered for PI-RADS 4 or 5, but not for PI-RADS 1 or 2"; for category 3 "biopsy may or may not be appropriate, depending on factors other than mpMRI alone"
Reporting, Findings, p. 7 (PSA density used in PI-RADS 3 biopsy decisions)

findings.piece: Quick Reference: action for PI-RADS 4 and 5 (and the calculator's results for 4 and 5)
findings.says: "PI-RADS 4 | High | Targeted biopsy recommended"; "PI-RADS 5 | Very high | Targeted biopsy strongly recommended". The calculator's results: "Targeted biopsy recommended." and "Targeted biopsy strongly recommended."

sources.location: Section III, p. 10 (PDF p. 17): "biopsy should be considered for PI-RADS 4 or 5" … "PI-RADS v2.1 does not include recommendations for management"
Targeted Biopsy Considerations, p. 8: targeted biopsy "either in addition to or instead of" systematic biopsy; at least 3 cores from index lesions
Recommendation 5a, p. E188: "If the mpMRI is positive, mpMRI-targeted biopsy (TB) and TRUS-guided systematic biopsy (TRUS-SB) should be performed together"

findings.fix: Say what PI-RADS says: biopsy should be considered for 4 and 5 (p. 10). Drop the "recommended" / "strongly recommended" grading, which no source gives, and "targeted" alone unless the page adopts a biopsy pathway.
findings.question: PI-RADS v2.1 makes no management recommendation, and CAR gives none by category. Should the page (and the calculator's results) keep an Action column at all? If so: PI-RADS's "biopsy should be considered for 4–5, not for 1–2", or the urology pathway CAR supports (CUA 2022 endorsing CCO 2021: targeted plus systematic biopsy when mpMRI is positive)?

findings.piece: Dominant sequence table: peripheral and transition zone rows
findings.says: "Peripheral Zone (PZ) | DWI | DCE"; "Transition Zone (TZ) | T2WI | DWI" (dominant, then secondary sequence).

sources.location: Caveats for Overall Assessment, p. 14 (PDF p. 21) ("For the PZ, DWI is the primary determining sequence"; "For the TZ, T2W is the primary determining sequence"); Section III, p. 10 (DCE may upgrade a PZ DWI 3); TZ table, p. 11

findings.piece: Dominant sequence table: central zone row
findings.says: "Central Zone | Assessed as part of TZ | —".

sources.location: Normal Anatomy, p. 7 (PDF p. 14): calling the TZ and CZ together the "central gland" "is discouraged"; Evaluation of the central zone, p. 14 (PDF p. 21): cancer starting in the CZ is uncommon, "most of these arise in either the adjacent PZ or TZ and extend into the CZ"; asymmetry or focal early enhancement may indicate cancer; Caveats, p. 15 (PDF p. 22): zonal location is vital, especially at "the interface of the CZ and PZ at the base"; Appendix II sector map, p. 31 (PDF p. 38): the CZ is its own zone
Slide "Major Revisions": "Further description of assessment of lesions in CZ and AFMS"

findings.fix: Replace with v2.1's text: the CZ is a separate zone, not part of the TZ; cancers there usually arise in the adjacent PZ or TZ, so the lesion's zone of origin decides the scoring table (as v2.1 states outright for the AFMS, p. 14); look for asymmetry and focal early enhancement.

findings.piece: Peripheral zone DWI table: scores 1–3
findings.says: "1 | No abnormality (homogeneous hyperintense on ADC and iso/hyperintense on high b-value DWI)"; "2 | Indistinct hypointense on ADC"; "3 | Focal mildly/moderately hypointense on ADC and iso/mildly hyperintense on high b-value DWI; <1.5 cm".

sources.location: PI-RADS Assessment of DWI, p. 20 (PDF p. 27): one table for PZ or TZ; 1 "No abnormality (i.e., normal) on ADC and high b-value DWI"; 2 "Linear/wedge shaped …"; 3 "Focal … may be markedly hypointense on ADC or markedly hyperintense on high b-value DWI, but not both" (no size)
Slide "Image Interpretation: DWI" (v2: 2 "Indistinct hypointense on ADC", 3 "Focal mildly/moderately hypointense on ADC and isointense/mildly hyperintense on high b-value DWI", no size)

findings.fix: Use v2.1's rows: 1 without the added parenthesis; 2 "Linear/wedge shaped hypointense on ADC and/or linear/wedge shaped hyperintense on high b-value DWI"; 3 "Focal hypointense on ADC and/or focal hyperintense on high b-value DWI; may be markedly one but not both", with no size limit (rows 2–3 are v2's wording, and "<1.5 cm" on 3 is in neither version). The table applies to both zones.

findings.piece: Peripheral zone DWI table: scores 4 and 5
findings.says: "4 | Focal markedly hypointense on ADC and markedly hyperintense on high b-value DWI; <1.5 cm"; "5 | As per 4 but ≥1.5 cm, or definite extraprostatic extension/invasive behavior".

sources.location: PI-RADS Assessment of DWI, p. 20 (PDF p. 27), scores 4 and 5 ("<1.5cm in greatest dimension"; "≥1.5cm in greatest dimension or definite extraprostatic extension/invasive behavior")

findings.fix: Optional: add "in greatest dimension" and the caveat that "markedly" means more than any other focus in the same zone (p. 21).

findings.piece: DCE role (PZ): what counts as positive and negative
findings.says: "DCE positive: Focal early enhancement (earlier than or simultaneously with adjacent normal tissue), used to upgrade DWI score 3 → PI-RADS 4"; "DCE negative: Does not change the DWI assessment".

sources.location: DCE section, pp. 21–22 (PDF pp. 28–29): positive is focal, earlier than or contemporaneous with adjacent normal tissue, "and corresponds to a finding on T2W and/or DWI"; DCE table, p. 22: negative includes diffuse multifocal enhancement not matching a focal finding and "focal enhancement corresponding to a lesion demonstrating features of BPH on T2WI (including features of extruded BPH in the PZ)"
Slide "Image Interpretation: DCE" (v2.1 modified the negative criteria; positive unchanged)

findings.fix: Define a positive DCE by all three conditions (focal; earlier than or with adjacent normal tissue; matching a suspicious T2W/DWI finding) and list v2.1's negatives, including focal enhancement of a BPH-type nodule extruded into the PZ, which must not upgrade a DWI 3.

findings.piece: DCE upgrade rule (PZ tip)
findings.says: "PZ DWI 3 + DCE positive → PI-RADS 4"; "PZ DWI 3 + DCE negative → PI-RADS 3".

sources.location: Section III, Peripheral Zone table, p. 11 (PDF p. 18)

findings.piece: Transition zone T2W table: scores 1 and 2
findings.says: "1 | Normal-appearing TZ (homogeneous intermediate signal); or round/well-defined hypointense nodule (BPH nodule)"; "2 | Circumscribed hypointense or heterogeneous signal intensity but well-defined margins".

sources.location: PI-RADS Assessment for T2W, TZ, p. 18 (PDF p. 25): 1 "Normal appearing TZ (rare) or a round, completely encapsulated nodule (\"typical nodule\")"; 2 "A mostly encapsulated nodule OR a homogeneous circumscribed nodule without encapsulation (\"atypical nodule\") OR a homogeneous mildly hypointense area between nodules"; Evaluation of the TZ, p. 13 (PDF p. 20) (typical BPH is T2W 1; incompletely or almost completely encapsulated nodules are T2W 2); Lexicon "Encapsulated", p. 33 (PDF p. 40) (completely encapsulated = in at least two planes)
Slide "Assessment of T2W" (v2: 1 "Homogeneous intermediate signal intensity (normal)", 2 "Circumscribed hypointense or heterogeneous encapsulated nodule(s) (BPH)")

findings.fix: Use v2.1's rows. Encapsulation, not hypointensity, separates them: a round, completely encapsulated nodule of any signal is 1; a mostly encapsulated nodule, a homogeneous circumscribed unencapsulated nodule, or a homogeneous mildly hypointense area between nodules is 2 (and becomes 3 with DWI 4 or 5).

findings.piece: Transition zone T2W table: scores 3–5
findings.says: "3 | Heterogeneous signal intensity with obscured margins (includes others not qualifying as 2, 4, or 5)"; "4 | Lenticular or non-circumscribed, homogeneous, moderately hypointense; <1.5 cm"; "5 | As per 4 but ≥1.5 cm, or definite extraprostatic extension/invasive behavior".

sources.location: PI-RADS Assessment for T2W, TZ, p. 18 (PDF p. 25), scores 3–5

findings.piece: DWI role (TZ) and DWI upgrade rule (TZ tip)
findings.says: "DWI 4 or 5: Upgrade T2WI 3 → PI-RADS 4"; "DWI 1, 2, or 3: Does not change T2WI assessment"; tip "TZ T2WI 3 + DWI ≥4 → PI-RADS 4", "TZ T2WI 3 + DWI ≤3 → PI-RADS 3".

sources.location: Section III, Transition Zone table, p. 11 (PDF p. 18) (T2W 3: DWI ≤4 → 3, DWI 5 → 4; T2W 2: DWI ≥4 → 3); Evaluation of the TZ, pp. 13–14 (PDF pp. 20–21)
Slide "Image Interpretation: Transition Zone" (v2 and v2.1 tables)

findings.fix: Replace with v2.1: T2W 3 becomes 4 only with DWI 5 (DWI 4 stays 3); T2W 2 becomes 3 with DWI 4 or 5 (DWI ≤3 stays 2); DWI does not change T2W 1, 4 or 5.

findings.piece: Flowchart: overall score assignment
findings.says: Rendered flowchart "Overall PI-RADS Score Assignment": PZ "DWI = 3 → DCE positive? Yes → PI-RADS 4 / No → PI-RADS 3", "DWI = 1, 2, 4, or 5 → PI-RADS = DWI score"; TZ "T2WI = 3 → DWI ≥ 4? Yes → PI-RADS 4 / No → PI-RADS 3", "T2WI = 1, 2, 4, or 5 → PI-RADS = T2WI score".

sources.location: Section III, Peripheral and Transition Zone tables, p. 11 (PDF p. 18)
Slide "Image Interpretation: Transition Zone"

findings.fix: Keep the PZ branch. TZ: T2W 2 → "DWI ≥4?" → 3 / else 2; T2W 3 → "DWI = 5?" → 4 / else 3; T2W 1, 4, 5 → that score. Optionally add the "DWI inadequate" branch (p. 16).

findings.piece: Anatomic zones table
findings.says: "Peripheral Zone (PZ) | Posterior/lateral, base to apex | ~70% | ~70% of PCa"; "Transition Zone (TZ) | Surrounding urethra, central gland | ~20–30% | ~20–30% of PCa"; "Central Zone (CZ) | Surrounding ejaculatory ducts at base | ~5% | Rare"; "Anterior Fibromuscular Stroma (AFMS) | Anterior | N/A | Rare".

sources.location: Normal Anatomy, p. 7 (PDF p. 14): TZ "contains 5% of the glandular tissue", CZ "about 20%", PZ "70%–80%" (the TZ grows with BPH); "Approximately 70-75% of prostate cancers originate in the PZ and 20-30% in the TZ"; CZ cancers uncommon, usually invasion by PZ tumours; "central gland" discouraged; AFMS "contains no glandular tissue"; p. 14 (PDF p. 21): "PCa does not originate in the AFMS"

findings.fix: Glandular tissue: PZ 70–80%, CZ about 20%, TZ 5% (more with BPH); cancer origin: PZ 70–75%, TZ 20–30%, CZ uncommon; AFMS has no glands and no cancer starts there. Drop "central gland".

findings.piece: Extraprostatic extension indicators table
findings.says: "Capsular bulge or irregularity | Suspicious for EPE"; "Broad capsular contact (≥1 cm) | Higher EPE risk"; "Obliteration of rectoprostatic angle | Suspicious for EPE"; "Neurovascular bundle asymmetry | Suspicious for involvement"; "Tumor abutting seminal vesicle | Seminal vesicle invasion risk".

sources.location: Section V Staging, p. 25 (PDF p. 32): asymmetry or invasion of the neurovascular bundles, bulging contour, irregular or spiculated margin, obliteration of the rectoprostatic angle, "a tumor-capsule interface of greater than 1.0 cm", breach of the capsule with direct tumour extension, bladder wall invasion; Lexicon, Staging terms, p. 38 (PDF p. 45): "Tumor-capsule abutment of greater than 1 cm"; broad base of contact "at least 25% of tumor contact with the capsule"

findings.fix: Make the contact length ">1 cm" (not ≥), add breach of the capsule with direct extension and bladder wall invasion, and replace "tumor abutting seminal vesicle" with the source's obliteration of the prostate–seminal vesicle angle or direct extension into the seminal vesicle.

findings.piece: Seminal vesicle invasion box
findings.says: "Low T2/ADC signal within seminal vesicle + direct extension from primary tumor = SVI (T3b disease)".

sources.location: Section V Staging, p. 25 (PDF p. 32): SVI features are focal or diffuse low T2W signal and/or abnormal enhancement within or along the seminal vesicle, restricted diffusion, obliteration of the prostate–seminal vesicle angle, and direct tumour extension; Lexicon, p. 39 (PDF p. 46): three types (spread along the ejaculatory ducts, direct extraglandular extension, a separate metachronous deposit); p. 25: MRI separates ≤T2 from ≥T3 (T3b is not named)

findings.fix: List the p. 25 features and the three lexicon types instead of a two-feature rule (a separate deposit without direct extension is still SVI). "T3b" is TNM's stage, which PI-RADS does not give; keep it only with a TNM citation.

findings.piece: PSA density formula
findings.says: "PSAD = PSA (ng/mL) / Prostate Volume (cc)".

sources.location: Section III A, Measurement of the Prostate Gland, p. 12 (PDF p. 19) ("PSAD=PSA/prostate volume")
Reporting, Findings, p. 7 ("PSA divided by prostate volume")

findings.piece: PSA density bands for PI-RADS 3
findings.says: "<0.10 | Low risk; biopsy may be deferred in PI-RADS 3"; "0.10–0.15 | Intermediate; shared decision-making for PI-RADS 3"; "≥0.15 | Higher risk; supports biopsy recommendation for PI-RADS 3".

sources.location: Reporting, Findings, p. 7: "in patients with PI-RADS 3 lesions, PSA density thresholds of approximately 0.1 to 0.15 have been suggested for biopsy" (no reference given for the sentence)
Section III, p. 10 (PDF p. 17) (for category 3, biopsy depends on factors other than MRI); PI-RADS gives no PSA density threshold

PSA density, p. E189: "A PSAD threshold of >0.15 ng/ml/cm3 has been suggested"; "the use of PSAD alone for clinical decision-making is discouraged; however, use of PSAD can be considered adjunctively in men with known prostate volumes"

findings.fix: Optional: cite CAR (p. 7) and present 0.10–0.15 as CAR does, a range of suggested biopsy thresholds for PI-RADS 3, rather than as named risk bands; add CUA 2022 (>0.15, not to be used alone) under "Other guidelines differ".

findings.piece: Prostate volume measurement tip
findings.says: "Use ellipsoid formula: V = 0.52 × AP × TR × CC (all in cm)".

sources.location: Section III A, Measurement of the Prostate Gland, p. 12 (PDF p. 19): maximum AP and longitudinal dimensions on the mid-sagittal T2W image, maximum transverse on the axial T2W image, × 0.52; manual or automated segmentation also acceptable
Reporting, Findings, p. 7 (AP and CC off the mid-sagittal image, transverse off the axial; state whether ellipsoid or volumetric)

findings.fix: Optional: add where each diameter is measured (AP and CC on the mid-sagittal T2W image, transverse on the axial T2W image) and that segmentation is acceptable (state which was used).

findings.piece: PSA density calculator
findings.says: Fields "PSA (ng/mL)" and "Prostate Volume (cc)"; result "PSA Density: <value> ng/mL/cc — <band>", the value rounded to three decimals. Runs (docs/audit/batch-2/cases/psa_density.results.md): 0.099 → Low; 0.100 → Intermediate; 0.149 → Intermediate; 0.150 and 0.151 → Higher; the document's example (PSA 12.1, 42 cc) → 0.288 (document: 0.29). Rounding moves edge values: PSA 4.99 / 50 cc (0.0998) → "0.1 … Intermediate risk"; PSA 7.49 / 50 cc (0.1498) → "0.15 … Higher risk". Volume 0, blank or negative → "Error: Prostate volume must be greater than 0." A blank, zero or negative PSA returns a density (0, 0, −0.02) with "Low risk. Biopsy may be deferred in PI-RADS 3 lesions."

sources.location: Section III A, p. 12 (PDF p. 19) (PSAD = PSA / volume); Appendix I example, p. 28 (PDF p. 35) ("42 cubic cm, PSA density 0.29 ng/mL/mL")
Reporting, Findings, p. 7 (0.1 to 0.15 for PI-RADS 3)

findings.fix: Compare the unrounded value with the bands (or round to two decimals and say the bands apply to that), and refuse a missing, zero or negative PSA instead of returning "Low risk".

findings.piece: Technique: T2W minimum standard
findings.says: "T2WI | ≥3 planes; slice thickness ≤3 mm; in-plane resolution ≤0.7 mm".

sources.location: T2W Technical Specifications, pp. 17–18 (PDF pp. 24–25): axial plus at least one orthogonal plane; "Slice thickness: 3mm, no gap"; FOV 12–20 cm; "In plane dimension: ≤0.7mm (phase) x ≤0.4mm (frequency)"
Imaging Acquisition Parameters, p. 6: T2W "in the axial plane and both sagittal and coronal planes" (sagittal may be a rapid sequence); "maximum recommended slice thickness of 3 mm"

findings.fix: Keep three planes (CAR p. 6; PI-RADS's minimum is two) and 3 mm with no gap; make the in-plane limit ≤0.7 mm (phase) × ≤0.4 mm (frequency).

findings.piece: Technique: DWI minimum standard
findings.says: "DWI | Include b = 0 and b ≥ 800 s/mm²; calculate ADC map; optional high b-value (b ≥ 1400 s/mm²)".

sources.location: DWI Technical Specifications, p. 19 (PDF p. 26): for the ADC map, a low b of 0–100 (preferably 50–100) and an intermediate b of 800–1000, maximum b for ADC ≤1000; "a high b-value (≥1,400 sec/mm2) image set is also mandatory" (acquired or calculated); TE ≤90 ms, TR ≥3000 ms, slice ≤4 mm no gap, FOV 16–22 cm, in-plane ≤2.5 mm
Imaging Acquisition Parameters, p. 6: low b 50–100 and intermediate b 800–1000; "a high b-value image of > 1400 s/mm2 is required"
Slide "Image Acquisition: DWI"

findings.fix: High b-value images (≥1400 s/mm², acquired or calculated) are mandatory, not optional; build the ADC map from a low b of 50–100 (CAR; PI-RADS allows 0–100) and an intermediate b of 800–1000, with no b above 1000 in the ADC fit.

findings.piece: Technique: DCE minimum standard
findings.says: "DCE | Temporal resolution ≤15 sec; spatial coverage of entire prostate".

sources.location: DCE Technical Specifications, p. 22 (PDF p. 29): temporal resolution ≤15 s; FOV encompassing the prostate and seminal vesicles; 3D T1W GRE preferred; slice 3 mm; in-plane ≤2 × 2 mm; observation >2 min; fat suppression and/or subtraction
Imaging Acquisition Parameters, p. 6: 3D T1-weighted GRE; temporal resolution ≤15 s

findings.fix: Optional: cover the seminal vesicles too and add 3D GRE, observation over 2 minutes and fat suppression or subtraction (p. 22).

findings.piece: Technique: field strength and endorectal coil
findings.says: "3T preferred — higher SNR and spatial resolution"; "1.5T acceptable — endorectal coil may improve quality"; "Endorectal coil not required at 3T with modern phased-array surface coils".

sources.location: Section I B, Magnetic Field Strength and Endorectal Coil, pp. 5–6 (PDF pp. 12–13)

Hardware Considerations, p. 4: 3T "whenever possible"; 1.5T for devices conditional only at 1.5T or degrading artefact (hip prosthesis); below 1.5T not recommended; endorectal coils "not necessary", may help large patients

findings.fix: Optional: use CAR's wording (3T unless contraindicated, nothing below 1.5T, endorectal coil not necessary at either strength).

findings.piece: Reporting template elements
findings.says: "1. Technique: Field strength, coil type, sequences performed; 2. Prostate: Volume, PSA density (if PSA available), overall gland appearance; 3. Lesion description (for each PI-RADS ≥ 3): Location (zone, sector per 27-sector map), Size (cm), DWI score, T2WI score, DCE result, Overall PI-RADS score, EPE suspicion; 4. Lymph nodes; 5. Seminal vesicles; 6. Incidental findings; 7. Overall impression: Most significant PI-RADS score; clinical management recommendation".

sources.location: Reporting, pp. 6–7: indication with patient age, date and PSA level, prior biopsies and therapies; technique stating PI-RADS v2.1 compliance, field strength, coil, enough to tell biparametric from multiparametric, the high b-value and image quality; size L × W × H with volume method and PSA density; haemorrhage and nodular hyperplasia; up to four lesions in order with the v2.1 sector map and series/image numbers, PZ size on ADC and TZ on T2W; T2W, DWI, DCE and overall scores; capsule, seminal vesicles, bladder neck and neurovascular bundles; nodes and bones with pertinent negatives; impression lists every lesion PI-RADS ≥3 and disease outside the capsule; Table 1, p. 3, recommendations 1 and 3 (image quality reported; PSA, age and indication in all reports); Appendix E template

Mapping and measurement of lesions, pp. 12–13 (PDF pp. 19–20) (up to four lesions of category 3–5, index lesion, sequence and image number of the measurement); Appendix I, pp. 26–27 (PDF pp. 33–34) (state PI-RADS compliance; PSA and prior biopsy; dates of prior exams)

findings.fix: Punctate echogenic foci do not shadow (a shadowing focus is a macrocalcification, 1 point, not 3); they may have small comet-tail artifacts. Add that the points for every type present are added.

findings.piece: Measurement Guidelines: size measurement
findings.says: "Use maximum diameter in any plane"; "Measure in centimeters (to one decimal)"; "Include solid and cystic components"; "Benign features (TR1-TR2): No size threshold"; "Always measure at largest diameter"; "Document plane of measurement".

sources.location: in-press PDF p6, Measurement and Documentation: "the maximum dimension determines whether a given lesion should be biopsied or followed"; "Nodules should be measured in three axes: (1) maximum dimension on an axial image, (2) maximum dimension perpendicular to the previous measurement on the same image, and (3) maximum longitudinal dimension on a sagittal image"; "Measurements should also include the nodule's halo, if present"; Fig 1 (p3): TR1–TR2 "No FNA" with no size limit

findings.fix: Optional: replace "any plane"/"document plane" with ACR's three axes, and add that the halo is included. "To one decimal" is not in the white paper.

findings.piece: Measurement Guidelines: definition of significant growth
findings.says: "Significant growth: >20% in two dimensions AND >2mm"; "Use same measurement technique".

sources.location: in-press PDF p6, Definition of Growth: "significant enlargement is defined as a 20% increase in at least two nodule dimensions and a minimal increase of 2 mm, or a 50% or greater increase in volume"; "it is important to also review measurements from earlier scans"; Timing of Follow-Up Sonograms: imaging stops at 5 years only "if there is no change in size"; nodules that enlarge but stay below the FNA threshold at 5 years: "continued follow-up is probably warranted"

findings.fix: "A 20% increase in at least two dimensions with a minimum increase of 2 mm, or a 50% or greater increase in volume"; compare with the earliest available scan, not only the last. The missing volume criterion can make a growing nodule look stable and end follow-up at 5 years.

findings.piece: Measurement Guidelines: "Minimum interval: 6 months"
findings.says: Under Growth Assessment: "Minimum interval: 6 months".

sources.location: in-press PDF p6, Timing of Follow-Up Sonograms: "The committee believes that scanning intervals of less than 1 year are not warranted, except for proven cancers under active surveillance, which may require more frequent follow-up at the discretion of the referring physician"

findings.fix: Follow-up scans are at least 1 year apart (except proven cancers under active surveillance, at the referring physician's discretion).

findings.piece: When NOT to use TI-RADS: age

findings.piece: Clinical correlation: suspicious lymphadenopathy
findings.says: "Clinical correlation required for: … Suspicious lymphadenopathy".

sources.location: in-press PDF p7, Assessment of Cervical Lymph Nodes: "Evaluation of cervical lymph nodes is a vital part of every thyroid sonographic examination"; suspicious features: globular shape, loss of the echogenic hilum, peripheral rather than hilar flow, heterogeneity with cystic components, punctate echogenic foci; "We recommend FNA of suspicious nodes, in addition to up to two nodules that warrant biopsy on the basis of the ACR TI-RADS"

findings.fix: Assess the cervical nodes at every thyroid ultrasound and recommend FNA of suspicious nodes (listing ACR's features), in addition to up to two nodules that meet TI-RADS criteria.

findings.piece: Clinical correlation: growth, symptoms, thyroglobulin, PET

findings.question: Keep this list as local practice, or replace it with ACR's general line on clinical factors?

findings.piece: Reporting Tips: structured report contents
findings.says: "Structured Report Should Include: Overall thyroid size and echogenicity; Number of nodules; For each nodule requiring characterization: Location (lobe, upper/mid/lower); Size (3 dimensions); Composition (points); Echogenicity (points); Shape (points); Margin (points); Echogenic foci (points); Total TI-RADS points and level; Recommendation based on size and TR level".

sources.location: in-press PDF p6, Measurement and Documentation: three-axis size; location "right, left, isthmus, upper, mid, lower, and, if necessary, lateral, medial, anterior, or posterior"; "no more than four nodules with the highest ACR TI-RADS point scores that fall below the size threshold for FNA should be followed"; Number of Nodules to Biopsy (p6–7): "targeting no more than two nodules with the highest ACR TI-RADS point totals that meet criteria for FNA. Size should not be the primary criterion"

findings.fix: Add ACR's limits: number and label each followed nodule, follow at most four (highest points) below the FNA threshold, and biopsy at most two (highest points, not the largest). Gland size and echogenicity are not in the white paper.

sources.location: in-press PDF p3, Fig 1: solid 2, hypoechoic 2, wider-than-tall 0, lobulated or irregular 2, punctate echogenic foci 3 (sum 9); "7 Points or More" TR5, "FNA if ≥ 1 cm" (1.8 cm)

findings.piece: Common Pitfalls: scoring errors
findings.says: "Don't add multiple features from same category"; "Don't upgrade based on size alone"; "Don't confuse macrocalcifications with punctate foci".

sources.location: in-press PDF p2, Overview: "the reader selects one feature from each of the first four categories and all the features that apply from the final category and sums the points"; in-press PDF p3, Fig 1: ECHOGENIC FOCI "(Choose All That Apply)"; p5, Echogenic Foci

findings.fix: "Choose one feature in each of the first four categories; for echogenic foci, add the points of every type present." The other two lines are consistent with the white paper.

findings.says: "Don't include halo in measurement"; "Don't measure only transverse plane"; "Don't round up aggressively".

sources.location: in-press PDF p6, Measurement and Documentation: "Measurements should also include the nodule's halo, if present"; three axes, the third "maximum longitudinal dimension on a sagittal image"

findings.fix: Include the halo in the measurement. The second line is right; the third is not from the white paper.

findings.says: "Don't FNA nodules below size threshold"; "Don't ignore clinical context"; "Don't apply to cervical lymph nodes".

findings.fix: Optional: "Don't routinely FNA nodules below the threshold (5–9 mm TR5: shared decision)"; add "Don't biopsy more than two nodules, and choose them by points, not size".

findings.piece: Adverse Reaction Classification, "Acute Reactions (within 1 hour)" tab: timing and severity grades (Severity and Symptoms columns)
findings.says: "Acute Reactions (within 1 hour)"; "Mild | Limited urticaria, nausea/vomiting, pruritus, pallor/diaphoresis"; "Moderate | Diffuse urticaria, mild bronchospasm, facial edema, tachycardia/bradycardia"; "Severe | Diffuse bronchospasm, laryngeal edema, anaphylactic shock, cardiac arrest".

sources.location: p2: "Acute or immediate HRs occur within 1 hour of exposure"; p3: the severity grades are the ACR's, reproduced in Appendix A, p11 (allergic-like and physiologic columns); Recommendation 2, p9: "It is important to distinguish between a true hypersensitivity reaction and a physiological reaction"; Figure 1, p10: mild–moderate and severe reactions take different paths

Table 1, Categories of Acute Reactions, pp95–96 (PDF pp98–99): mild allergic-like — limited urticaria/pruritis, cutaneous edema, limited "itchy"/"scratchy" throat, nasal congestion, sneezing/conjunctivitis/rhinorrhea; mild physiologic — limited nausea/vomiting, transient flushing/warmth/chills, headache/dizziness/anxiety/altered taste, mild hypertension, vasovagal reaction that resolves spontaneously. Moderate allergic-like — diffuse urticaria/pruritis, diffuse erythema with stable vital signs, facial edema without dyspnea, throat tightness or hoarseness without dyspnea, wheezing/bronchospasm with mild or no hypoxia; moderate physiologic — protracted nausea/vomiting, hypertensive urgency, isolated chest pain, vasovagal reaction that requires and is responsive to treatment. Severe allergic-like — diffuse edema or facial edema with dyspnea, diffuse erythema with hypotension, laryngeal edema with stridor and/or hypoxia, wheezing/bronchospasm with significant hypoxia, anaphylactic shock (hypotension + tachycardia); severe physiologic — vasovagal reaction resistant to treatment, arrhythmia, convulsions/seizures, hypertensive emergency; cardiopulmonary arrest a nonspecific end stage

findings.fix: Use the ACR grades as CAR/CSACI reproduce them, with allergic-like and physiologic reactions apart: facial edema is moderate only without dyspnea (with dyspnea, severe); bronchospasm is graded by hypoxia; "pallor/diaphoresis" and "tachycardia/bradycardia" are not grades in the source (hypotension with bradycardia is vasovagal, with tachycardia anaphylactic shock). The 1-hour window is right.

findings.piece: Adverse Reaction Classification, "Acute Reactions" tab: Treatment column
findings.says: "Mild … | Observation, diphenhydramine if hives are bothersome"; "Moderate … | Diphenhydramine, consider epinephrine if bronchospasm"; "Severe … | Epinephrine (IM), oxygen, IV fluids, call emergency services".

sources.location: Treatment of Contrast Reactions, p86 (PDF p89): mild reactions typically need no treatment; observe a mild allergic-like reaction "for a minimum of 20 to 30 minutes"; an antihistamine may be given for symptomatic urticaria. Table 3, pp104–108 (PDF pp107–111): mild hives — diphenhydramine 25–50 mg PO or fexofenadine 180 mg PO; bronchospasm (mild and moderate) — beta-agonist inhaler first, moderate "Consider adding epinephrine"; severe reactions — epinephrine IV 0.1 mg (1 mL of 0.1 mg/mL) or IM 0.3 mg; note on each epinephrine row: "in hypotensive patients, the preferred route of epinephrine delivery is IV"

p3: management "usually including second generation antihistamines for mild reactions, and intramuscular epinephrine and cardiorespiratory support for more severe reactions"; Appendix B, p12: the CSACI no longer recommends first-generation antihistamines such as diphenhydramine

findings.fix: Moderate bronchospasm starts with a beta-agonist inhaler (albuterol), adding epinephrine if needed; severe reactions with hypotension take IV epinephrine (0.1 mg of 0.1 mg/mL) when there is IV access, IM 0.3 mg otherwise. Mild: observe 20–30 minutes; an oral antihistamine if symptomatic (CAR/CSACI: second-generation).

findings.piece: "Delayed Reactions (1–72 hours)" tab
findings.says: "Delayed Reactions (1–72 hours)": "Predominantly skin reactions (maculopapular rash, urticaria)"; "Usually self-limited; treat with oral antihistamines or steroids if needed"; "Incidence: ~2% after ionic, ~1% after non-ionic contrast".

sources.location: p3: delayed HRs "occur hours to days after exposure", are usually mild isolated skin reactions, maculopapular exanthem the most common, with rare severe cutaneous reactions (AGEP, DRESS, SJS/TEN); Frequency, p3: 5725 delayed HRs in 11 712 796 LOCM administrations (0.05%); p6: "premedication for delayed HRs is not recommended"

Delayed Adverse Events, pp28–29 (PDF pp31–32): reactions "may develop from 30 to 60 minutes to up to one week following contrast material exposure, with the majority occurring between three hours and two days"; incidence of delayed allergic-like reactions "0.5% to 14%"; treatment supportive, "antihistamines and/or corticosteroids used for cutaneous symptoms"

findings.fix: The window is hours to days (ACR: 30–60 minutes up to a week, most between 3 hours and 2 days), not 1–72 hours. Drop the ionic/non-ionic incidence (no source; CAR/CSACI give 0.05% for LOCM). The skin and treatment lines are right; add that severe cutaneous reactions are rare and premedication for delayed reactions is not recommended (CAR/CSACI p6).

findings.piece: "Late Reactions (>72 hours)" tab
findings.says: "Late Reactions (>72 hours)": "Thyroid dysfunction (contrast-induced hyperthyroidism) — especially with high iodine load"; "Metformin-related lactic acidosis risk".

sources.location: No ">72 hours" category: delayed reactions run up to one week (pp28–29, PDF pp31–32); thyrotoxicosis after iodinated contrast in patients with a history of hyperthyroidism is "rare" (Patient Selection, p6, PDF p9); metformin is not a reaction — contrast is "a concern only if post-contrast acute kidney injury (AKI) should develop" (Metformin, p44, PDF p47)
pp2–3: hypersensitivity reactions are immediate (within 1 hour) or delayed (hours to days); no later category

findings.fix: Drop the tab: neither source has a >72-hour category; the thyroid belongs in the thyroid section and metformin in the metformin section.

findings.piece: Acute Contrast Reaction Treatment, "Urticaria (Mild)" tab
findings.says: "1. Observe patient"; "2. If symptomatic: Diphenhydramine 25–50 mg IV/IM"; "3. If extensive: consider escalation".

sources.location: Table 3, Hives, p104 (PDF p107): mild (scattered and/or transient) — "No treatment often needed; however, if symptomatic, can consider: Diphenhydramine (Benadryl®) 25–50 mg PO or Fexofenadine (Allegra®) 180 mg PO"; moderate — the same oral options or diphenhydramine 25–50 mg IM or IV ("administer IV dose slowly over 1–2 min"); severe (widespread and/or progressive) — diphenhydramine 25–50 mg IM or IV; footnote: "IM/IV form may cause or worsen hypotension". Treatment of Contrast Reactions, p86 (PDF p89): observe mild allergic-like reactions at least 20 to 30 minutes
p3: second-generation antihistamines for mild reactions; Appendix B, p12: first-generation antihistamines no longer recommended; the only IV antihistamine available in Canada is first-generation (p4)

findings.fix: Mild hives take an oral antihistamine, not IV/IM: diphenhydramine 25–50 mg PO or fexofenadine 180 mg PO (CAR/CSACI prefer a second-generation one such as fexofenadine). IM/IV diphenhydramine 25–50 mg (IV over 1–2 minutes) is for moderate or severe hives. Observe at least 20–30 minutes.

findings.piece: Acute Contrast Reaction Treatment, "Bronchospasm" tab
findings.says: "1. Oxygen via face mask (6–10 L/min)"; "2. Albuterol (beta-2 agonist) inhaler — 2–3 puffs; may repeat"; "3. If no improvement or severe: Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM (1:1,000) in anterolateral thigh"; "4. Call emergency services if severe".

sources.location: Table 3, Bronchospasm, p106 (PDF p109): O2 by mask 6–10 L/min; beta-agonist inhaler (Albuterol®) "2 puffs (90 mcg/puff) for a total of 180 mcg; can repeat up to 3 times"; moderate — "Consider adding epinephrine (IM)": 0.3 mL of 1.0 mg/mL (1:1,000) (0.3 mg), "can repeat every 5-15 minutes up to 1 mL (1 mg) total", or IV 1 mL of 0.1 mg/mL (1:10,000) (0.1 mg), repeat every few minutes up to 10 mL (1 mg) total; severe — epinephrine IV (listed first) or IM, AND the inhaler, and "Call emergency response team or 911". No injection site is given

findings.fix: Albuterol is 2 puffs (90 mcg each, 180 mcg), repeatable up to 3 times, not 2–3 puffs (a small difference). Add the IM epinephrine limit (every 5–15 minutes, up to 1 mg total) and the IV option (0.1 mg of 0.1 mg/mL slowly, up to 1 mg). Oxygen and the 0.3 mg IM dose are right.

findings.piece: Acute Contrast Reaction Treatment, "Laryngeal Edema" tab
findings.says: "1. Oxygen via face mask"; "2. Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM (1:1,000) — may repeat every 5–15 min"; "3. Call emergency services immediately"; "4. Prepare for possible intubation".

sources.location: Table 3, Laryngeal Edema, p107 (PDF p110): O2 by mask 6–10 L/min; epinephrine IV 1 mL of 0.1 mg/mL (1:10,000) (0.1 mg), repeat every few minutes up to 1 mg total, or IM 0.3 mL of 1.0 mg/mL (1:1,000) (0.3 mg), "can repeat every 5-15 minutes up to 1 mL (1 mg) total", or auto-injector 0.3 mg up to three times; "Consider calling emergency response team or 911 based upon the severity of the reaction and the completeness of the response"

findings.fix: The IM dose, concentration and interval are right. Add oxygen 6–10 L/min, the 1 mg total limit and the IV option; "prepare for possible intubation" is not in the ACR table.

findings.piece: Acute Contrast Reaction Treatment, "Anaphylaxis / Anaphylactic Shock" tab
findings.says: "1. Call emergency services (Code Blue)"; "2. Epinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg IM (1:1,000) — anterolateral thigh; may repeat every 5–15 min"; "3. Supine position (legs elevated if tolerated)"; "4. Oxygen via face mask (10–15 L/min)"; "5. IV access; normal saline 1–2 L bolus for hypotension"; "6. Diphenhydramine 25–50 mg IV (adjunct only, NOT primary treatment)"; "7. If refractory: epinephrine infusion, vasopressors".

sources.location: Table 3, Hypotension (systolic < 90 mm Hg), p108 (PDF p111): all forms — O2 by mask 6–10 L/min, "Elevate legs at least 60 degrees", "IV fluids 0.9% normal saline 1,000 mL rapidly" or lactated Ringer's 1,000 mL; hypotension with tachycardia (anaphylactoid), if hypotension persists — epinephrine IV 1 mL of 0.1 mg/mL (1:10,000) (0.1 mg) slowly into a running infusion, repeat every few minutes up to 10 mL (1 mg) total, or IM 0.3 mL of 1.0 mg/mL (1:1,000) (0.3 mg), repeat every 5–15 minutes up to 1 mL (1 mg) total; note: "in hypotensive patients, the preferred route of epinephrine delivery is IV". Hives footnote, p104 (PDF p107): IM/IV diphenhydramine "may cause or worsen hypotension". Reaction Rebound Prevention, p111 (PDF p114): IV corticosteroids "not useful in the acute treatment of any reaction"
p3: "intramuscular epinephrine and cardiorespiratory support for more severe reactions" (no doses)

findings.fix: Per ACR Table 3: epinephrine IM 0.3 mg (not 0.3–0.5 mg), every 5–15 minutes to 1 mg total, or IV 0.1 mg (1 mL of 0.1 mg/mL) slowly, repeated to 1 mg, preferred when hypotensive with IV access; oxygen 6–10 L/min (not 10–15); 1,000 mL saline or lactated Ringer's rapidly (not 1–2 L); legs raised at least 60 degrees. IV diphenhydramine is not in the ACR's shock treatment, which warns it can worsen hypotension.
findings.question: If your practice uses a local anaphylaxis protocol (for example epinephrine 0.5 mg IM), should the page give it, labelled local practice, instead of the ACR dose?

findings.piece: Acute Contrast Reaction Treatment, "Vasovagal Reaction" tab
findings.says: "1. Elevate legs (Trendelenburg position)"; "2. Oxygen if needed"; "3. IV fluids for hypotension"; "4. Atropine 0.6–1 mg IV if persistent bradycardia".

sources.location: Table 3, Hypotension, p108 (PDF p111): all forms — O2 by mask 6–10 L/min, "Elevate legs at least 60 degrees", 0.9% saline or lactated Ringer's 1,000 mL rapidly; hypotension with bradycardia (pulse < 60 bpm) (vasovagal): mild — no other treatment usually necessary; severe (symptomatic despite the above) — atropine IV "0.6–1.0 mg; administer into a running IV infusion of fluids; can repeat up to 3 mg total"; consider calling the emergency response team

findings.fix: Raise the legs at least 60 degrees; Trendelenburg (head-down tilt) is not what the ACR says. The atropine dose is right; add "into a running IV infusion, repeat up to 3 mg total, if symptomatic despite legs, oxygen 6–10 L/min and 1,000 mL fluid".

findings.piece: Premedication for High-Risk Patients: "Who Needs Premedication?" — prior-reaction indications and the no-guarantee note
findings.says: "Prior moderate or severe acute allergic-like reaction to same class of contrast agent"; "Multiple prior mild reactions to same class"; note "No premedication proven to eliminate risk entirely".

sources.location: Recommendations 3, 5, 6, 7 and 10, pp9–11, and Figure 1, p10: after a mild, moderate or severe hypersensitivity reaction to LOCM or GBCA, switching to a chemically different agent "is the single best protective measure"; steroid premedication is not recommended ("This practice should be discontinued", Rec 5); a second-generation oral antihistamine at least 1 hour before is optional after a mild or moderate reaction (Rec 7); after anaphylaxis or a severe reaction, consider another modality or an allergist, otherwise switch agent and monitor, "Premedication is not recommended" (Rec 10). Recommendation 4 and Figure 2: unknown iodinated culprit agent

Indications for Premedication, p9 (PDF p12): 12- or 13-hour oral or accelerated IV premedication "may be considered" for a prior allergic-like or unknown-type reaction to the same class, of any severity; a prior severe reaction is a relative contraindication to the same class. Changing Contrast Media Within the Same Class, p10 (PDF p13). Premedication Is Not a Panacea, p11 (PDF p14)
The 2025 update for unknown contrast agents (not readable)

findings.fix: Under the CAR/CSACI lead: after a reaction of any severity, switch to a chemically different agent; no steroid premedication; an optional second-generation antihistamine (oral, at least 1 hour before) after mild or moderate reactions; after severe reactions, consider another modality or an allergist. The ACR's indication is any prior allergic-like or unknown-type reaction to the same class (not only moderate/severe; "multiple mild" is not an ACR criterion). The no-guarantee note is right in both.
findings.question: For patients with a prior contrast reaction, does your practice follow CAR/CSACI 2025 (switch agent, no steroids) or the ACR's premedication? The unknown-agent part of CAR/CSACI was updated in 2025 (copy requested from you).
findings.home: Prior contrast reaction › Other guidelines differ

findings.piece: Premedication indications: "History of asthma"
findings.says: "History of asthma (increased risk of severe reactions)", listed under "Who Needs Premedication?".

sources.location: Patient Selection, p5 (PDF p8): "Due to the modest increased risk, restricting contrast medium use or premedicating solely on the basis of a history of asthma is not recommended"; p9 (PDF p12): routine premedication for asthma "is not recommended"

Recommendation 2, p9: patients are at risk only after a previous hypersensitivity reaction to the same type of agent; "There is insufficient evidence to support routine screening of other risk factors"

findings.fix: Remove asthma as an indication: the ACR and CAR/CSACI both advise against premedicating for asthma alone.

findings.piece: Standard Premedication Regimens, "Elective (13-hour)" tab (methylprednisolone)
findings.says: "Methylprednisolone | 32 mg PO | 13 hours before"; "Methylprednisolone | 32 mg PO | 1 hour before"; "Diphenhydramine (optional) | 50 mg PO/IM/IV | 1 hour before".

sources.location: Specific Recommended Premedication Regimens, pp9–10 (PDF pp12–13): "Methylprednisolone-based: 32 mg methylprednisolone by mouth 12 hours and 2 hours before contrast medium administration. 50 mg diphenhydramine may be added as in option 1"; the 13-hour regimen is the prednisone one (13, 7 and 1 hours); diphenhydramine "may be considered optional"
Recommendations 5 and 6, pp10–11: steroid premedication not recommended for prior reactions to LOCM or GBCA

findings.fix: The ACR's methylprednisolone regimen is 32 mg PO at 12 and 2 hours before (not 13 and 1), and it is the 12-hour regimen. Under the CAR/CSACI lead it moves to "Other guidelines differ".
findings.question: Follows the lead choice asked on B2-contrast-safety-11.

findings.piece: Standard Premedication Regimens, "Alternative (12-hour)" tab (prednisone)
findings.says: "Prednisone | 50 mg PO | 13 hours before"; "Prednisone | 50 mg PO | 7 hours before"; "Prednisone | 50 mg PO | 1 hour before"; "Diphenhydramine (optional) | 50 mg PO | 1 hour before".

sources.location: Specific Recommended Premedication Regimens, pp9–10 (PDF pp12–13): "Prednisone-based: 50 mg prednisone by mouth at 13 hours, 7 hours, and 1 hour before contrast medium administration, plus 50 mg diphenhydramine intravenously, intramuscularly, or by mouth 1 hour before"; diphenhydramine "may be considered optional"; if oral medication is not possible, hydrocortisone 200 mg IV for each prednisone dose
Recommendations 5 and 6, pp10–11: steroid premedication not recommended

findings.fix: Matches the ACR's prednisone regimen, which is the 13-hour one (the "12-hour" label belongs to methylprednisolone); diphenhydramine may be IV, IM or PO. Under the CAR/CSACI lead it moves to "Other guidelines differ".

findings.piece: Standard Premedication Regimens, "Accelerated (3–5 hour)" tab and its warning
findings.says: "Methylprednisolone | 40 mg IV | Every 4 hours until contrast"; "Diphenhydramine | 50 mg IV | 1 hour before"; warning "Accelerated regimens are less effective — use only when 12-hour regimen is not feasible".

sources.location: Accelerated IV Premedication, p10 (PDF p13): methylprednisolone sodium succinate 40 mg IV or hydrocortisone sodium succinate 200 mg IV "immediately, and then every 4 hours until contrast medium administration, plus diphenhydramine 50 mg IV 1 hour before"; "This regimen usually is 4-5 hours in duration"; dexamethasone 7.5 mg IV for methylprednisolone allergy; "Premedication regimens less than 4-5 hours in duration (oral or IV) have not been shown to be effective". Indications, p9 (PDF p12): accelerated IV when 12- or 13-hour premedication would delay care, or an outpatient arrives unpremedicated
p4: a 5-hour IV regimen had a breakthrough rate (2.5%) non-inferior to the 13-hour oral regimen (2.1%); Recommendations 5 and 6, pp10–11: steroid premedication not recommended

findings.fix: The duration is 4–5 hours ("3–5 hour" includes regimens with no evidence); the first dose is given immediately; hydrocortisone 200 mg IV is an alternative (dexamethasone 7.5 mg IV for methylprednisolone allergy). "Less effective" is not in the ACR; the 5-hour IV regimen was non-inferior in the study CAR/CSACI cite. Under the CAR/CSACI lead it moves to "Other guidelines differ".

findings.piece: Contrast and Renal Function: "Risk Stratification for CI-AKI" note and the eGFR ≥45 row
findings.says: "True CI-AKI is less common than historically believed. Risk is primarily significant in patients with severely reduced GFR."; "≥45 | Low | Contrast may be given; no additional precautions".

sources.location: Chronic Kidney Disease section: "Only those with severe CKD (eGFR ≤30 mL/min/1.73 m2), and those with preexisting AKI are at risk of CA-AKI"; Summary of recommendations 3a (eGFR >30 and no AKI: proceed) and 8 (no oral or IV hydration for eGFR >30); Table 1: CA-AKI is the general term, CI-AKI only where contrast is the proven cause

PC-AKI chapter, p37 (PDF p40): "very little evidence that IV iodinated contrast material is an independent risk factor for AKI in patients with eGFR ≥30"; p40 (PDF p43): prophylaxis "not indicated for the general population of patients with stable eGFR greater than or equal to 30"

findings.fix: Correct; CAR 2022 uses "contrast-associated AKI (CA-AKI)" for this risk, keeping CI-AKI for proven causation.

findings.piece: Contrast and Renal Function: the eGFR 30–44 row
findings.says: "30–44 | Moderate | IV hydration if feasible; consider benefit vs. risk".

sources.location: Summary of recommendations 3a (eGFR >30 and no AKI: "proceed with an indicated contrast imaging study") and 8 ("We do not recommend oral or IV hydration for patients with eGFR >30 mL/min/1.73 m2, receiving IV ICM or IA ICM"); Table 2: CAR 2012's bands (30–44 "moderate risk", preventive measures below 45) were replaced in 2022

PC-AKI chapter, p40 (PDF p43): prophylaxis "is not indicated for the general population of patients with stable eGFR greater than or equal to 30"; it "may also be considered on an individual basis for high-risk circumstances (e.g. numerous risk factors, recent AKI, borderline eGFR) in patients with an eGFR of 30-44 … at the discretion of the ordering provider"

findings.fix: Under CAR 2022, eGFR >30 with no AKI: proceed, with no hydration and no risk band. (The ACR allows hydration at 30–44 only case by case in high-risk circumstances; the "moderate" band is CAR's 2012 scheme.)

findings.piece: Contrast and Renal Function: the eGFR <30 (not on dialysis) row
findings.says: "<30 (not on dialysis) | Elevated | Use with caution; discuss with ordering physician; IV hydration".

sources.location: Summary of recommendations 3a: eGFR ≤30 or suspected AKI — "an individual patient decision involving the caring team or patient/patient decision maker"; 2a: emergent studies proceed without delay; 9: IV ICM at eGFR ≤30 — "the working group makes no recommendation" on volume expansion, "institutions may choose practices best suited to their local environments"; 10: IA ICM at eGFR ≤30 — hydration (0.9% saline or 1.26% sodium bicarbonate IV, or oral salt and water) left to the practitioner
PC-AKI chapter, pp39–40 (PDF pp42–43): "Prophylaxis is indicated for patients who have AKI or severe CKD with an eGFR less than 30"; isotonic saline preferred

findings.fix: Use CAR's cut-off (≤30, or suspected AKI) and its individual decision with the care team; for IV contrast say hydration is a local choice (CAR makes no recommendation); emergent studies are not delayed.
findings.question: For eGFR ≤30 with IV contrast, does your practice give IV hydration? CAR leaves it to each institution; if it does, the page labels it local practice.

findings.piece: Contrast and Renal Function: the "Dialysis-dependent" row
findings.says: "Dialysis-dependent | N/A | Contrast may be given; coordinate dialysis timing if possible".

sources.location: Chronic dialysis patients section and Summary of recommendations 3b: "Imaging with ICM can be performed in patients on peritoneal or hemodialysis regardless of residual urine output and no change in dialysis schedule is required"; 12: no post-contrast dialysis; Table 2: the 2012 guidance also called coordination with hemodialysis "unnecessary"

PC-AKI chapter, p40 (PDF p43): patients should not have dialysis initiated or "alter their schedule solely based on iodinated contrast media administration"; dialysis patients making more than 1–2 cups (100 mL) of urine a day are treated as high-risk

findings.fix: Contrast may be given with no change to the dialysis schedule (CAR and ACR). The ACR's high-risk handling of non-anuric dialysis patients differs from CAR, for whom residual urine output does not change the decision.

findings.piece: Contrast and Renal Function: "IV Hydration Protocol" tab
findings.says: "For patients at risk (eGFR 30–44 or risk factors)": "Normal saline 100 mL/hr IV — 6 hours before and 6 hours after contrast, OR"; "Sodium bicarbonate 1.26% solution 3 mL/kg/hr × 1 hour before, then 1 mL/kg/hr × 6 hours after (alternative)".

sources.location: Summary of recommendations 8–10; Hydration or Volume Expansion section: bicarbonate "does not provide any added benefit" over normal saline, which "would be the preferable option"; oral or IV hydration may be used; Table 4: the Merten bicarbonate protocol ran "over 1 hour pre-procedure and 4 hours post-procedure"; PRESERVE found bicarbonate no better than saline

PC-AKI chapter, p39 (PDF p42): "Typical prophylaxis regiments begin 1 hour prior to the exam and continue 3-12 hours after"; fixed volume (e.g. 500 mL NS) before and after, or 1–3 mL/kg per hour; Solomon et al: 100 mL/h from 12 hours before to 12 hours after; p40 (PDF p43): bicarbonate "not preferred"

findings.fix: Under CAR 2022 there is no hydration for eGFR >30; at ≤30 hydration is a local choice (IV contrast) or the practitioner's (IA), normal saline preferred, oral acceptable. The page's rates and durations (6 hours before and after; bicarbonate for 6 hours after) are in neither source; if kept, label them local practice.
findings.question: Follows the hydration question on B2-contrast-safety-18.

findings.piece: Contrast and Renal Function: "N-Acetylcysteine" tab
findings.says: "Not recommended — evidence does not support use for CI-AKI prevention."

sources.location: Summary of recommendations 13: "We do not recommend NAC use for the prophylaxis of CA-AKI"; N-acetylcysteine section: "strong evidence against prophylactic use of NAC"
PC-AKI chapter, p40 (PDF p43): N-acetylcysteine "is therefore not recommended for intravenous contrast media prophylaxis"

findings.piece: Metformin Guidelines table: the "≥30" and "<30 OR acute kidney injury expected" rows
findings.says: "Current ACR guidance:"; "≥30 (intra-arterial or intravenous) | No need to hold metformin — low risk in hemodynamically stable patients with eGFR ≥30"; "<30 OR acute kidney injury expected | Hold metformin at time of contrast; do not restart for 48 hours; recheck renal function before resuming".

sources.location: Summary of recommendations 16 ("We do not recommend stopping metformin before contrast injection, and/or retesting kidney function afterward, for patients with eGFR >30 mL/min/1.73 m2") and 17 (eGFR ≤30 or AKI: held "at the time of, or prior to" ICM, "not restarted for at least 48 hours and only then if kidney function remains stable (<25% increase compared with baseline creatinine) and the ongoing use of metformin has been reassessed by the patient's clinical team"); Drug Interactions section: no route distinction

Metformin chapter, pp44–45 (PDF pp47–48): Category I — no AKI and eGFR ≥30, intravenous contrast: no need to discontinue; Category II — AKI, eGFR < 30, or "arterial catheter studies that might result in emboli (atheromatous or other) to the renal arteries": discontinue at or before the procedure, withhold 48 hours, reinstitute "only after renal function has been re-evaluated and found to be normal"

findings.fix: CAR continues metformin at eGFR >30 and holds it at ≤30 or with AKI (not "AKI expected"), so at eGFR 30 it is held; restart after at least 48 hours only if creatinine has risen <25% from baseline and the clinical team has reassessed. "Hemodynamically stable" is in neither source; the ACR holds metformin for arterial studies that might embolise to the kidneys whatever the eGFR.

findings.piece: Metformin Guidelines table: the "Intra-arterial contrast with eGFR 30–60" row
findings.says: "Intra-arterial contrast with eGFR 30–60 | Consider holding metformin; reassess renal function at 48 hours".

sources.location: Metformin chapter, pp44–45 (PDF pp47–48): no eGFR 30–60 band; Category II covers "arterial catheter studies that might result in emboli … to the renal arteries" at any eGFR (hold 48 hours, then re-evaluate)
Summary of recommendations 16: no stopping of metformin at eGFR >30, with no route distinction

findings.fix: Remove the row: neither source has an eGFR 30–60 band, and it contradicts the page's own first row. CAR continues metformin at eGFR >30 by any route; the ACR's exception is arterial studies with possible renal emboli (hold 48 hours, then reassess).

findings.piece: Gadolinium-Based Contrast Agents: NSF note, "NSF Risk Grouping" table and "Preferred Agents" tip
findings.says: "Nephrogenic Systemic Fibrosis (NSF) is a rare but serious fibrosing disorder in patients with severely reduced renal function."; "Group I (Highest) | Gadodiamide (Omniscan), gadoversetamide (OptiMARK), gadopentetate dimeglumine (Magnevist) | High — avoid in eGFR <30 or AKI"; "Group II (Moderate) | Gadobenate dimeglumine (MultiHance), gadofosveset (Ablavar) | Intermediate — caution in eGFR <30"; "Group III (Lowest) | Gadobutrol (Gadavist), gadoteridol (ProHance), gadoterate meglumine (Dotarem), gadoterate macrocyclic agents | Negligible — preferred in at-risk patients"; tip: "Use macrocyclic ionic or non-ionic agents (Group III) when GBCA is required in patients with eGFR <30."

sources.location: Not readable (copy requested from the owner)
Not readable (copy requested from the owner)

NSF chapter, Table 1, p80 (PDF p83): Group I — gadodiamide, gadopentetate dimeglumine, gadoversetamide; Group II ("few, if any, unconfounded cases of NSF") — gadobenate dimeglumine, gadobutrol, gadoteric acid (Dotarem, Clariscan), gadoteridol, gadopiclenol, gadoxetate disodium; Group III — "No agents currently in this category (as of April 2024)". pp76, 78–79 (PDF pp79, 81–82): Group I contraindicated on dialysis and in CKD 4–5 and avoided in AKI; "Group II agents are strongly preferred in patients at risk for NSF"
The 2025 NSF chapter (GBCA group clarification; not readable)

findings.fix: Against ACR 2024 the grouping is wrong: Group II is gadobenate, gadobutrol, gadoteric acid (gadoterate), gadoteridol, gadopiclenol and gadoxetate; Group III is empty; gadofosveset is not listed; Group II is preferred in at-risk patients. Group I and the NSF note are right. The verdict waits for CAR 2018/2019 and the ACR 2025 NSF chapter.
findings.question: CAR 2018 and its 2019 update lead here and copies have been requested from you (the publisher blocks download). Until they are read, should the page carry the ACR 2024 grouping?

findings.piece: "GBCA and Renal Function" table
findings.says: "≥30 | Standard doses of any GBCA are acceptable; Group III preferred"; "15–29 | Group III preferred; use lowest effective dose; document risk discussion"; "<15 or dialysis-dependent | Risk vs. benefit discussion required; Group III agents; avoid Group I/II"; "AKI | Avoid GBCA if possible; if necessary, Group III only".

sources.location: Not readable (copy requested from the owner)
Not readable (copy requested from the owner)

NSF chapter, pp78–79 (PDF pp81–82): CKD 3 (eGFR 30–59) "No special precautions are necessary"; CKD 1–2 "Any GBCA can be administered safely"; CKD 4–5 not on dialysis — Group I contraindicated, "a group II agent should be used"; chronic dialysis — Group I contraindicated, a Group II agent recommended, consider CT in anuric patients, elective GBCA MRI "as closely before a regularly scheduled hemodialysis as is possible", dialysis not initiated or altered; AKI — avoid Group I, "a group II agent is preferred"; informed consent not recommended before Group II; lowest dose, not above the single recommended dose (p78, PDF p81). Table 2, p80 (PDF p83): eGFR checks are for Group I or III agents
The 2025 NSF chapter (not readable)

findings.fix: Against ACR 2024: Group II (which includes the macrocyclics) is the agent for eGFR <30, dialysis and AKI, at the lowest diagnostic dose; "avoid Group I/II" on dialysis and "avoid GBCA if possible" in AKI contradict it, and no Group III agent exists. On dialysis, time elective scans just before a scheduled session without changing the schedule. The verdict waits for CAR 2018/2019.
findings.question: Follows the question on B2-contrast-safety-24.

findings.piece: GBCA and Special Populations, "Pregnancy" tab
findings.says: "Gadolinium crosses the placenta; association with adverse effects found in some epidemiologic studies"; "Use only when clearly necessary and benefit outweighs risk"; "Document informed consent discussion"; "Prefer lowest effective dose; avoid repeated exposure"; "MRI without contrast is preferred first for pregnant patients".

sources.location: Pregnancy chapter, pp88–89 (PDF pp91–92): a GBCA crosses the placenta (primates); a Canadian birth-database study found more stillbirth or neonatal death and rheumatological, inflammatory or infiltrative conditions; GBCAs "should only be used if their usage is considered critical and the potential benefits justify the potential unknown risk"; one of the agents at low risk for NSF "at the lowest possible dose"; confer with the referrer and document that the information cannot be obtained without contrast or by other modalities, affects care, and cannot wait; informed consent recommended. Gadolinium Pregnancy Screening Statement, p74 (PDF p77): avoid routine GBCA in pregnancy; screen for unsuspected pregnancy

findings.fix: Correct; add that a Group II (low NSF risk) agent is used and that the ACR recommends screening for unsuspected pregnancy before GBCA. "Avoid repeated exposure" is not stated in the ACR.

findings.piece: GBCA and Special Populations, "Lactation" tab
findings.says: "<0.04% of GBCA dose is excreted into breast milk; <1% of that is absorbed by infant"; "ACR guidance: GBCA administration is safe to continue breastfeeding; interruption is not necessary"; "However, if patient requests: may pump-and-discard for 24 hours for peace of mind".

sources.location: Breast-Feeding chapter, pp93–94 (PDF pp96–97): "Less than 0.04% of the intravascular dose given to the mother is excreted into the breast milk in the first 24 hours"; "less than 1% of the contrast medium ingested by the infant is absorbed" (systemic dose < 0.0004%); safe to continue; a concerned mother may abstain "for a period of 12 to 24 hours", expressing and discarding milk. Summary, Question 2, p92 (PDF p95)

findings.fix: Correct; the ACR's optional pause is 12 to 24 hours and is the mother's informed decision.

findings.piece: GBCA and Special Populations, "Iodinated Contrast in Pregnancy" tab
findings.says: "Iodinated contrast crosses the placenta; neonatal thyroid function may be transiently suppressed"; "Use only when clinically necessary"; "If administered: check neonatal thyroid function in first week after delivery".

sources.location: Pregnancy chapter, p88 (PDF p91): IV iodinated contrast "does not affect short-term neonatal thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH)"; "no documented case of neonatal hypothyroidism from the maternal intravascular injection of water-soluble iodinated contrast agents"; with routine newborn TSH screening "no extra attention is felt to be necessary"; no routine pregnancy screening before iodinated contrast; "We do not recommend withholding the use of iodinated contrast agents in pregnant or potentially pregnant patients when it is needed for diagnostic purposes". Patient Selection, p6 (PDF p9): a single maternal dose "has no effect on neonatal thyroid function"

findings.fix: Remove the neonatal thyroid check and the suppression claim: the ACR finds no effect on neonatal TSH and relies on routine newborn screening. Keep: it crosses the placenta and is given when needed for diagnosis.
findings.home: Contrast in pregnancy and breast-feeding › Management

findings.piece: GBCA and Special Populations, "Iodinated Contrast During Breastfeeding" tab
findings.says: "<1% of dose enters breast milk; <1% of that is absorbed"; "ACR guidance: Continue breastfeeding after iodinated contrast without interruption".

sources.location: Breast-Feeding chapter, p93 (PDF p96): "less than 1% of the administered maternal dose of iodinated contrast medium is excreted into the breast milk in the first 24 hours"; "less than 1% of the contrast medium ingested by the infant is absorbed" (systemic dose < 0.01%); safe to continue; an optional 12–24-hour pause is the mother's informed decision; no routine infant thyroid testing. Summary, Questions 1 and 3, p92 (PDF p95)

findings.piece: Contrast Extravasation: "Extravasation Management" table
findings.says: "Minor | <10 mL of iso-osmolar or <2 mL of high-osmolar | Minimal pain/swelling | Elevate extremity, ice packs 15–20 min several times/day; monitor"; "Significant | >10 mL of iso-osmolar or >2 mL of high-osmolar; hypo-osmolar agents; any volume with tissue ischemia symptoms | Marked swelling, blistering, vascular compromise | Elevate extremity, plastic surgery / wound care consultation; imaging if vascular compromise suspected".

sources.location: Extravasation summary, pp17–20 (PDF pp20–23): examine for tenderness, swelling, erythema, paresthesia, finger range of motion and perfusion; elevate above the heart; "Cold compresses or ice packs should initially be applied" (Question 4, Rec 2); no hyaluronidase, steroid injection or aspiration (Rec 3); "Surgical consultation should not be routinely requested based on volume alone" (Question 5, Rec 1, strength Strong); consult for severe pain, progressive swelling or pain, decreased capillary refill, change in sensation, worsening range of motion, or skin ulceration or blistering (Rec 2). Treatment, p22 (PDF p25): the volume thresholds some have used are 100 or 150 mL; consultation by signs and symptoms

findings.fix: Drop the volume bands (no source gives 10 mL or 2 mL; the ACR advises against volume triggers) and "hypo-osmolar agents". Elevate above the heart, cold compresses first, examine; urgent surgical consultation for severe or progressive pain or swelling, poor capillary refill, altered sensation, worsening range of motion, or blistering or ulceration. "15–20 min several times/day" and imaging are not in the ACR.

findings.piece: Contrast Extravasation: "Follow-up contact" line
findings.says: "Follow-up contact: Advise patients to return if symptoms worsen, paresthesia, or skin changes develop."

sources.location: Extravasation, Question 4, Rec 4, p19 (PDF p22): all discharged outpatients get clear instructions on when to seek care (worsening pain, paresthesia, diminished range of motion, new ulceration or blistering); Discharging Patients, p22 (PDF p25); Documentation, p24 (PDF p27)

findings.fix: Correct; the ACR also asks for an observation period before discharge, documentation, and notice to the referrer after a symptomatic extravasation.

findings.piece: Thyroid and Iodinated Contrast: thyrotoxicosis precautions (first three bullets)
findings.says: "Large doses of iodinated contrast can cause contrast-induced thyrotoxicosis in susceptible patients (autonomous nodules, Graves' disease)"; "Patients with known hyperthyroidism or autonomous nodules: discuss with ordering physician and endocrinology prior to administering high-dose iodinated contrast"; "Routine patients without known thyroid disease: no special precautions needed".

sources.location: Patient Selection, p6 (PDF p9): thyrotoxicosis after iodinated contrast in patients with a history of hyperthyroidism is "rare"; "restricting contrast medium use or premedicating solely on the basis of a history of hyperthyroidism is not recommended"; in acute thyroid storm iodinated contrast "should be avoided"; with normal thyroid function, contrast does not affect thyroid function tests

findings.fix: The ACR asks for no endocrinology discussion: hyperthyroidism alone is no reason to restrict contrast, but acute thyroid storm is a reason to avoid it (missing here). "Large doses", "autonomous nodules" and "Graves'" are not in the ACR; the no-precautions line is right.
findings.question: Is a discussion with endocrinology before high-dose contrast in hyperthyroid patients your local practice, to keep and label?
findings.home: Iodinated contrast and the thyroid › Management

findings.piece: Thyroid and Iodinated Contrast: radioactive iodine bullet
findings.says: "Contrast may interfere with radioiodine therapy — delay radioactive iodine treatment by 2–6 months after large contrast doses".

sources.location: Patient Selection, p6 (PDF p9): iodinated contrast "can interfere with uptake of the treatment and diagnostic dose"; "The washout period is ideally 3-4 weeks for patients with hyperthyroidism, and 6 weeks for patients with hypothyroidism"

findings.fix: The washout before radioactive iodine therapy or imaging is ideally 3–4 weeks in hyperthyroidism and 6 weeks in hypothyroidism, not 2–6 months, after any iodinated contrast dose.
findings.home: Iodinated contrast and the thyroid › Management

findings.piece: Contrast Reaction Risk Factors table
findings.says: "Prior reaction (same class) | Yes — major risk factor | Yes"; "Asthma | 2–3× increased risk | Slightly increased"; "Multiple allergies/atopy | Yes | Yes"; "Cardiac disease | For severe reactions | No"; "Renal impairment | CI-AKI risk | NSF risk"; "Anxiety | Yes (idiosyncratic) | No"; "Beta-blocker use | May worsen reaction, impairs epinephrine response | No".

sources.location: Recommendation 2, p9: only a previous hypersensitivity reaction to the same type of agent (LOCM–LOCM, GBCA–GBCA) marks a patient at risk; "There is insufficient evidence to support routine screening of other risk factors"; p3: a prior contrast reaction or asthma raises GBCA reaction risk 1.5 to 3 times

Patient Selection, pp5–6 (PDF pp8–9): a prior allergic-like reaction to the same class is about a 5-fold risk and the greatest risk factor; unrelated allergies 2- to 3-fold; asthma increases the likelihood (no figure); severe cardiac disease, anxiety and beta-blockers are discussed for contrast media generally; none is a reason to premedicate or restrict; no cross-reactivity between classes. GBCM chapter, p71 (PDF p74): asthma and other allergies a mild increased risk for GBCA

findings.fix: Under CAR/CSACI only a prior reaction to the same type of agent is screened; the rest can stay as background. The 2–3× figure is the ACR's for unrelated allergies, not asthma (for GBCA, CAR/CSACI give 1.5–3× for asthma); the "No" entries for GBCA (cardiac disease, anxiety, beta-blockers) have no source.

findings.piece: Common Pitfalls: reaction-treatment items
findings.says: Don't: "Treat contrast reactions with antihistamines alone — epinephrine is first-line for anaphylaxis"; "Delay epinephrine waiting for IV access — give IM first".

sources.location: Table 3, pp105 and 108 (PDF pp108, 111): epinephrine for hypotensive reactions, IV or "(if no IV access available)" IM; antihistamines appear only under hives; Reaction Rebound Prevention, p111 (PDF p114): corticosteroids "not useful in the acute treatment of any reaction"
p3: intramuscular epinephrine for more severe reactions

findings.fix: Correct; add that when IV access is in place, IV epinephrine is preferred in hypotension (ACR Table 3 note).

findings.piece: Common Pitfalls: gadolinium items
findings.says: Don't: "Use Group I/II GBCA agents in patients with eGFR <30 when alternatives exist"; Do: "Choose macrocyclic GBCA when renal function is compromised".

sources.location: Not readable (copy requested from the owner)

NSF chapter, pp78–80 (PDF pp81–83): a Group II agent (gadobenate, gadobutrol, gadoteric acid, gadoteridol, gadopiclenol, gadoxetate) is recommended at eGFR <30, on dialysis and in AKI; Group I contraindicated

findings.piece: Common Pitfalls: renal function and metformin items
findings.says: Don't: "Routinely hold metformin for eGFR ≥30 (outdated practice)"; Do: "Check eGFR and relevant medications before contrast".

sources.location: Summary of recommendations 1 (outpatients with no current eGFR and no kidney history: two screening questions; if both no, proceed without eGFR), 2 (inpatients: eGFR within 7 days; emergent: do not delay or withhold contrast for eGFR), 16 (no stopping metformin at eGFR >30), 18–19 (no routine stopping of ACE inhibitors, ARBs or diuretics)

findings.fix: Replace "check eGFR before contrast" with CAR's screen: eGFR for inpatients (within 7 days) or when the screening questions are positive, never delaying emergent studies; metformin is the only drug held (eGFR ≤30 or AKI), and it continues at eGFR >30, not ≥30.

findings.piece: Common Pitfalls: general "Do" items (preparedness, documentation, training)
findings.says: Do: "Have emergency medications and equipment immediately available in all contrast-administering areas"; "Document contrast type, dose, lot number, and any reactions in the medical record"; "Brief all imaging staff on acute reaction protocols".

sources.location: Table 4, p112 (PDF p115): equipment and medications within or near any room where contrast is injected; Treatment of Contrast Reactions, p86 (PDF p89): staff trained in recognising and treating reactions, with in-service training

findings.fix: Correct; add CAR/CSACI's detail: the precise agent name and dose, and for a reaction its onset, nature and treatment, also in the radiology report. Lot number is in neither source.

findings.piece: Emergency Equipment Checklist ("Required Emergency Supplies (Contrast Area)")

sources.location: Table 4, pp112–113 (PDF pp115–116): minimum equipment — access to oxygen (non-rebreather masks preferred), "Defibrillator or automated external defibrillator (AED)", blood pressure and pulse monitor, pulse oximeter, stethoscope; minimum medications — epinephrine IM 1 mg/1 mL, inhaled short-acting beta-agonist, an antihistamine; discretionary — suction, bag-valve-mask, normal saline and tubing, syringes and IV cannulas, epinephrine IV 1 mg/10 mL, atropine IV 1 mg/10 mL, IV corticosteroid, nitroglycerin 0.4 mg SL, aspirin 325 mg, furosemide 20–40 mg IV, labetalol 20 mg IV, dextrose 50%; post the emergency response number

findings.fix: Add the ACR's minimum items the "required" list lacks — a defibrillator or AED and a stethoscope — and mark atropine, saline and IV supplies as discretionary; "crash cart accessible within minutes" is not the ACR's standard. The other items are in Table 4.

usability.notes: About 40 words before the first field (title, the collapsed reference box's label, the open Purpose box, the heading). Four dropdowns (2, 5, 5 and 2 options), so the score definitions are hidden until a list is opened, and both score fields are asked for either zone. The upgrade rules sit below the form in second tabs ("DCE Role (PZ)", "DWI Role (TZ)") that need a click; the rendered flowchart further down is visible without clicks, but its TZ branch is wrong (B2-pi-rads-18). No option for an inadequate or absent sequence (category X).

The form sits about 520 visible words down the page, after the PI-RADS calculator, the score tables, flowchart, anatomy, EPE and the PSAD band table. Two number fields; the formula and bands are directly above it. Address-filled runs skip the fields' required and min=0 checks, so a blank or negative PSA returned "Low risk"; by the markup, typed blank or negative values should be stopped by the browser (not run), but a PSA of 0 is accepted and returns "Low risk".

13 words before the first field (heading, the collapsed reference box's label, "TI-RADS Calculator", the first label). Five drop-downs (18 options, points shown in each) and a size box, so options are hidden until opened. The Quick Reference table (levels, thresholds, intervals) is open just under the form and the points table is lower down without clicks, so the algorithm is visible, but the page runs to about 900 words and gives the levels three times (table, five cards, calculator text), with Measurement and Reporting tips collapsed. Echogenic foci is one drop-down where ACR adds every type; spongiform carries 0 like cystic and its rule is not applied; anechoic can be paired with a solid nodule. Size is in cm with step 0.1, so a typed 2.45 or a size in mm is refused or misread (from the markup, not run). Each result prints a malignancy risk the white paper does not give.
